q: Counting its overseas territories, how many time zones does France span - more than any other country?
fact: From French Polynesia to Wallis and Futuna, France's territories put it ahead of Russia's 11 time zones.

q: Which landmark in Paris, France, was built as the entrance arch to the 1889 World's Fair?
fact: It was only meant to stand for 20 years, and was saved because it proved useful as a radio antenna.

q: Which color jersey does the overall leader of the Tour de France wear?
fact: Green goes to the points leader, polka dots to the best climber and white to the best young rider.

q: Which famous monument did France give to the United States in 1886?
fact: Its iron skeleton was designed by Gustave Eiffel, a few years before he built his tower.

q: Which city in Germany hosts Oktoberfest, the world's largest folk festival?
fact: Despite its name, most of the festival takes place in September, ending on the first weekend of October.

q: In which year did the Berlin Wall open, paving the way for the reunification of Germany?
fact: The wall had divided the city since 1961. Germany was formally reunited on October 3, 1990.

q: Which composer, born in Bonn, Germany, wrote the 'Ode to Joy' melody now used as the anthem of Europe?
fact: It comes from his Ninth Symphony, finished in 1824 when he was almost completely deaf.

q: Which invention by Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz, Germany, around 1450 made books far cheaper to produce?
fact: His first major work was a Bible. Around 180 copies were printed, and 49 of them still survive.

q: How many independent countries are completely surrounded by Italy?
fact: San Marino and Vatican City are both entirely enclosed by Italian territory.

q: Which city in Italy is considered the birthplace of pizza?
fact: The Margherita is said to have been named in 1889 for Queen Margherita, with toppings in the colors of the Italian flag.

q: Which volcano on the island of Sicily in Italy erupts so often that it ranks among the most active in the world?
fact: At roughly 3,400 meters, Etna changes height with every major eruption.

q: Which city in Italy is built on more than 100 small islands linked by canals and about 400 bridges?
fact: Its buildings stand on millions of wooden piles driven into the mud of the lagoon centuries ago.

q: Which church in Barcelona, Spain, designed by Antoni Gaudí, has been under construction for more than 140 years?
fact: Work began in 1882. Its tallest tower was only finished in 2026, and Gaudí himself is buried in the crypt.

q: What happens at La Tomatina, a festival held every August in Buñol, Spain?
wrong: A race in front of bulls
fact: Around 20,000 people throw more than 100 tons of overripe tomatoes at each other in about an hour.

q: Which language spoken in northern Spain is unrelated to any other known living language?
fact: Basque, or Euskara, was spoken in the region long before Latin arrived with the Romans.

q: Which two football clubs from Spain meet in the match known as 'El Clásico'?
fact: The two clubs first played each other in 1902, and the game is now among the most-watched club matches in the world.

q: What is the popular name of the flag of the United Kingdom?
fact: It combines the crosses of Saint George, Saint Andrew and Saint Patrick.

q: Which sport's oldest tournament has been played at Wimbledon in the United Kingdom since 1877?
fact: It is the only one of the four Grand Slam tournaments still played on grass.

q: How many countries make up the United Kingdom?
fact: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Great Britain is only the first three.

q: Which prehistoric stone circle stands on Salisbury Plain in the United Kingdom?
fact: Its big sarsen stones weigh about 25 tons on average, and the smaller bluestones were hauled about 240 km from Wales.

q: Which lake in Russia is the deepest in the world and holds about a fifth of Earth's unfrozen surface fresh water?
fact: Baikal is more than 1,600 meters deep and around 25 million years old.

q: The Trans-Siberian Railway in Russia is the longest railway line in the world. Roughly how long is it?
fact: The journey from Moscow to Vladivostok takes about seven days without a stopover.

q: What are matryoshkas, a famous souvenir from Russia?
fact: The first set was carved in 1890 and is said to have been inspired by a nesting doll from Japan.

q: Which city in Russia was founded by Peter the Great in 1703 and served as the capital for about two centuries?
fact: Built on marshland along the Neva River, it has also been called Petrograd and Leningrad.

q: Portugal is the world's largest producer of which natural material, used to seal bottles?
fact: Cork is bark stripped from cork oaks about every nine years, without cutting the tree down.

q: Which explorer from Portugal led the first European voyage to reach India by sea, in 1498?
fact: He sailed around Africa's Cape of Good Hope, opening a sea route for the spice trade.

q: What is a 'pastel de nata', a famous treat from Portugal?
fact: The recipe is credited to monks in the Belém district of Lisbon, where a bakery has sold the tarts since 1837.

q: The Netherlands has more of which vehicle than it has people?
fact: Around 23 million bikes share the country with about 18 million people.

q: Which flower set off a famous buying frenzy in the Netherlands in the 1630s?
fact: At the peak of 'tulip mania', a single rare bulb was said to sell for the price of a house.

q: Why is orange the national color of the Netherlands?
answer: The name of its royal family
wrong: The roofs of its old towns
The sails of its trading ships
fact: The royal House of Orange-Nassau descends from William of Orange, who led the Dutch revolt in the 16th century.

q: In Sweden, what is 'fika'?
answer: A coffee break with a pastry
wrong: A midsummer dance around a pole
A sauna followed by a cold swim
fact: Many Swedish workplaces pause for fika twice a day, often with a cinnamon bun.

q: Which pop group from Sweden won the Eurovision Song Contest in 1974 with the song 'Waterloo'?
fact: The name is made from the first letters of its four members: Agnetha, Björn, Benny and Anni-Frid.

q: A famous hotel in Jukkasjärvi, Sweden, is rebuilt every winter out of what?
fact: The ice blocks are cut from the frozen Torne River, and the rooms stay at about -5°C.

q: What is the 'midnight sun' that draws summer visitors to northern Norway?
answer: The sun stays up all night
wrong: A total eclipse of the sun
Green lights in the night sky
A full moon over the fjords
fact: North of the Arctic Circle the sun does not set at all for weeks around midsummer.

q: Which artist from Norway painted 'The Scream'?
fact: Munch made four versions of it between 1893 and 1910, in paint and in pastel.

q: What is stored in the Global Vault built deep inside a frozen mountain on Svalbard, Norway?
fact: The vault holds more than a million seed samples as a backup for gene banks around the world.

q: What is unusual about the shape of the national flag of Switzerland?
wrong: It is taller than it is wide
fact: Vatican City is the only other country with a square national flag.

q: Which city in Switzerland is home to the International Olympic Committee?
fact: The IOC moved there in 1915, and the city now calls itself the Olympic Capital.

q: Which sweet treat was invented in Switzerland in 1875 by Daniel Peter?
fact: He succeeded after years of trials, with help from his neighbor Henri Nestlé, a maker of milk-based baby food.

q: Which humanitarian organization, founded in Geneva, Switzerland, in 1863, uses the Swiss flag with its colors reversed?
fact: Its founder, Henry Dunant, shared the very first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901.

q: In which year did Athens, Greece, host the first modern Olympic Games?
fact: About 240 athletes from 14 nations took part, and the winners received silver medals, not gold.

q: Which mountain in Greece did the ancient Greeks believe was the home of their gods?
fact: At 2,917 meters it is also the highest mountain in the country.

q: Which ancient temple dedicated to the goddess Athena crowns the Acropolis in Athens, Greece?
fact: Finished in 432 BC, it once held a huge gold-and-ivory statue of Athena.

q: Which musical instrument is the national emblem of Ireland, shown on its coins and passports?
fact: The emblem is modeled on a medieval harp kept at Trinity College Dublin. Guinness uses the same harp, facing the other way.

q: Which ancient stick-and-ball game is a national sport of Ireland and is often called the fastest game on grass?
fact: The ball, called a sliotar, can fly at more than 150 km/h.

q: According to legend, which animals did Saint Patrick drive out of Ireland?
fact: In reality Ireland has had no native snakes since the last Ice Age.

q: Which composer, born in Salzburg, Austria, in 1756, wrote more than 600 works before dying at 35?
fact: He began composing at the age of five and toured the courts of Europe as a child prodigy.

q: What is a Wiener schnitzel, a classic dish of Austria?
fact: Under Austrian food rules, only a schnitzel made from veal may be sold as a Wiener schnitzel.

q: Which dynasty ruled Austria for more than 600 years, until 1918?
fact: At its height the family also ruled Spain, Hungary, Bohemia and much of the Americas.

q: Which fried food does Belgium claim to have invented, serving it in paper cones with mayonnaise?
fact: Belgium has thousands of fry stands, known as friteries or frietkoten.

q: Which comic-book reporter with a white dog named Snowy was created in Belgium in 1929?
fact: His creator, Hergé, sent him to the Moon in a story published about 15 years before Apollo 11.

q: What does the Atomium, a landmark in Brussels, Belgium, represent?
wrong: The planets of the solar system
fact: Built for the 1958 World's Fair, it shows an iron crystal magnified 165 billion times.

q: Which toy brand, named after the Danish words for 'play well', was founded in Denmark in 1932?
fact: The modern brick was patented in 1958, and bricks made then still fit the ones sold today.

q: Which record does the Dannebrog, the flag of Denmark, hold?
answer: Oldest national flag still in use
wrong: First flag flown at the South Pole
Most colors of any national flag
fact: According to legend it fell from the sky during a battle in 1219.

q: Which author from Denmark wrote 'The Little Mermaid' and 'The Ugly Duckling'?
fact: A bronze Little Mermaid has sat on a rock in Copenhagen harbor since 1913.

q: Which scientist, born in Warsaw, Poland, was the first person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences?
fact: She named the element polonium after her homeland.

q: What can visitors see deep inside the Wieliczka mine near Kraków, Poland?
fact: Over some 700 years, miners carved chapels, statues and even chandeliers from the rock salt.

q: Which animal, the heaviest land mammal in Europe, roams the Białowieża Forest in Poland?
fact: Wiped out in the wild by the 1920s, it was bred back from just a dozen animals kept in zoos.

q: How do most people in Iceland get their last name?
wrong: From the farm they were born on
From a list approved by the church
fact: Jón's son is Jónsson and his daughter is Jónsdóttir, so phone books are sorted by first name.

q: What natural source heats about nine out of ten homes in Iceland?
fact: Hot water from underground is piped straight into homes, and even under some sidewalks to melt the snow.

q: The Althing of Iceland, founded in the year 930, is often called the world's oldest surviving what?
fact: It first met outdoors at Thingvellir, in a rift valley between two tectonic plates.

q: Finland has more than 3 million of what - roughly one for every two people?
fact: Saunas are found in homes, offices, lakeside cabins and even inside the parliament building.

q: Finland is called the 'land of a thousand lakes'. About how many lakes does it really have?
fact: That count includes every lake larger than 500 square meters, about the size of two tennis courts.

q: Which unusual sport holds its world championships every summer in Sonkajärvi, Finland?
fact: Competitors race over a 253.5-meter obstacle course, usually carrying their partner upside down on their back.

q: Which colorful puzzle was invented in Hungary in 1974 by a professor of architecture?
fact: Ernő Rubik needed about a month to solve his own invention for the first time.

q: Which lake in Hungary is the largest in Central Europe by surface area?
fact: Hungarians call it their 'sea'. It is 77 km long but only about 3 meters deep on average.

q: To which language family does Hungarian, the language of Hungary, belong - unlike those of all its neighbors?
fact: Its best-known relatives are Finnish and Estonian, although speakers cannot understand one another.

q: Which creature appears in black on the red flag of Albania?
fact: It comes from the banner of the national hero Skanderbeg, and Albanians call their home the 'Land of the Eagles'.

q: Albania built more than 170,000 of which structures across the country between the 1960s and 1980s?
fact: Many of the small domes still dot fields and beaches, and some are now cafes, museums or guesthouses.

q: Andorra has two heads of state called co-princes. One is a Spanish bishop - who is the other?
fact: The arrangement dates from 1278, which makes every French president a prince for as long as the term lasts.

q: What is the only official language of Andorra?
fact: Andorra is the only country in the world where Catalan is the sole official language.

q: What is the main ingredient of draniki, a national dish of Belarus?
fact: The grated potato pancakes are fried until crisp and usually served with sour cream.

q: Which huge vehicles is the BelAZ factory in Belarus famous for building?
fact: Its BelAZ-75710 can carry about 450 tons, roughly the weight of a fully loaded jumbo jet.

q: What do daring divers traditionally leap from in the town of Mostar, Bosnia and Herzegovina?
wrong: A waterfall on the Una River
fact: The Old Bridge, first built in 1566 and rebuilt in 2004, rises more than 20 meters above the Neretva River.

q: Which international event did Sarajevo, now the capital of Bosnia and Herzegovina, host in 1984?
fact: The mascot of the Games was Vučko, a cartoon wolf from the mountains around the city.

q: What is unusual about nodding and shaking the head in Bulgaria?
answer: A nod means no, a shake means yes
wrong: Nodding is only for greeting elders
Shaking the head means thank you
fact: Visitors often get it wrong, and many Bulgarians switch gestures when they talk to foreigners.

q: Which flower, harvested in a famous valley near Kazanlak in Bulgaria, yields a prized perfume oil?
fact: It takes more than three tons of petals, picked by hand at dawn, to make a single kilogram of rose oil.

q: Which item of clothing traces its origins to Croatia - its French name 'cravate' comes from the word for Croat?
fact: Croatian soldiers in 17th-century Paris wore knotted neck scarves that became a fashion at the French court.

q: What is Plitvice, the oldest national park of Croatia, famous for?
fact: Its 16 lakes are linked by waterfalls that keep growing as minerals in the water build natural dams.

q: What makes the flag of Cyprus unusual among national flags?
answer: It shows a map of the country
wrong: It is a single solid color
fact: The outline is copper-colored, recalling the metal that takes its very name from the island.

q: Which firm cheese from Cyprus can be grilled or fried without melting?
fact: It is traditionally made from goat's and sheep's milk and often flavored with mint.

q: Which record does Prague Castle in the Czech Republic hold, according to Guinness World Records?
fact: The complex covers about 70,000 square meters and has been a seat of rulers since the 9th century.

q: Which word, now used worldwide, comes from 'R.U.R.', a 1920 play by a writer from today's Czech Republic?
fact: Karel Čapek took it from 'robota', meaning forced labor - an idea he credited to his brother Josef.

q: Which everyday item was invented in 1961 by chemist Otto Wichterle in what is now the Czech Republic?
fact: He made the first ones at home on a machine built from a children's construction kit and a bicycle dynamo.

q: Which internet calling service was built by programmers in Estonia and launched in 2003?
fact: Started by a Swede and a Dane with Estonian engineers, it helped turn Tallinn into a startup hub.

q: In 2005 Estonia became the first country in the world to let its citizens do what online nationwide?
fact: In the 2023 parliamentary election, more than half of all votes were cast over the internet.

q: Which pop star, whose parents come from Pristina in Kosovo, released the hit album 'Future Nostalgia'?
fact: Born in London, she spent part of her teens in Pristina and later co-founded the city's Sunny Hill Festival.

q: How many white stars arc above the golden map on the flag of Kosovo?
fact: The six stars stand for the six main ethnic communities living in the country.

q: Riga, the capital of Latvia, has one of the world's finest collections of buildings in which style?
fact: About a third of the buildings in the city center date from the Art Nouveau boom around 1900.

q: Riga in Latvia claims to be where which holiday tradition began, in 1510?
fact: Tallinn in Estonia makes a rival claim, dating its own first tree to 1441.

q: Liechtenstein is one of only two 'doubly landlocked' countries in the world. What does that mean?
wrong: It has no rivers or lakes at all
It is ringed by two mountain chains
fact: The other one is Uzbekistan. From Liechtenstein you must cross at least two borders to reach a sea.

q: Tiny Liechtenstein is often described as a world leader in making which product?
fact: The dental company Ivoclar, based in the town of Schaan since 1933, ships artificial teeth to more than 100 countries.

q: Which sport is so loved in Lithuania that it is often called the country's second religion?
fact: Lithuania won the European title in 1937, 1939 and 2003, and three Olympic bronze medals in a row from 1992.

q: What covers a famous hill near Šiauliai in Lithuania that draws pilgrims from around the world?
fact: Nobody knows the exact number, but estimates run well above 100,000 crosses.

q: In 2020 Luxembourg became the first country in the world to make what free for everyone?
fact: Standard-class trains, trams and buses across the whole country need no ticket, for residents and tourists alike.

q: Luxembourg is the only country in the world whose head of state holds which title?
fact: It has been a grand duchy since 1815.

q: The stone temples of Malta are among the oldest free-standing buildings on Earth. About how old are the oldest?
fact: The Ġgantija temples on the island of Gozo were built around 3600 BC, about a thousand years before the pyramids of Giza.

q: Maltese, the national language of Malta, descends mainly from which language?
fact: It is the only Semitic language with the Latin alphabet as its standard script, and an official language of the EU.

q: The Mileștii Mici cellars in Moldova hold a Guinness record for the world's largest collection of what?
fact: More than 1.5 million bottles rest in underground galleries so long that the corridors have street names.

q: Moldova is landlocked, yet it has a port at Giurgiulești on a short stretch of which river?
fact: The country's bank of the Danube is only about half a kilometer long, but it links Moldova to the Black Sea.

q: What is special about the Formula 1 Grand Prix held in Monaco?
wrong: It is raced entirely at night
It is run on a gravel track
fact: First run in 1929, it is the slowest race on the calendar and one of the most famous.

q: Monaco is the second-smallest country in the world. Roughly how large is it?
fact: It is smaller than Central Park in New York, yet home to nearly 40,000 people.

q: What does the name Montenegro mean?
fact: The name comes from Venetian Italian. In the local language the country is Crna Gora, with the same meaning.

q: About how deep is the Tara River Canyon in Montenegro, one of the deepest canyons in Europe?
fact: The Tara is nicknamed the 'Tear of Europe' for its clear water, and rafting down the canyon is a popular trip.

q: Which Nobel Peace Prize winner was born in 1910 in Skopje, today the capital of North Macedonia?
fact: A memorial house in the city center stands on the site of the church where she was baptized.

q: Lake Ohrid in North Macedonia is one of Europe's deepest lakes and also one of its what?
fact: It is thought to be more than a million years old and has about 200 species found nowhere else.

q: Which fictional vampire was partly inspired by Vlad the Impaler, a 15th-century prince from what is now Romania?
fact: Author Bram Stoker never visited Romania. He researched Transylvania in British libraries.

q: Which record does the Palace of the Parliament in Bucharest, Romania, hold?
fact: It contains about 700,000 tons of steel and bronze and a million cubic meters of marble.

q: What did gymnast Nadia Comăneci of Romania become the first to achieve at the 1976 Olympics?
wrong: Five gold medals in one Games
A win at the age of 12
fact: The scoreboard could not show 10.00, so it displayed 1.00 instead. She was 14 years old.

q: San Marino traces its founding to the year 301. Which title does it claim as a result?
fact: Tradition says it was founded by Marinus, a stonemason who took refuge on Mount Titano.

q: San Marino is led by two heads of state called Captains Regent. How long is their term?
fact: A new pair takes office every April 1 and October 1, a custom that goes back to 1243.

q: Serbia is one of the world's leading exporters of which fruit?
fact: Most are grown on small family farms in western Serbia, around towns such as Arilje, and sold frozen.

q: The main airport of Belgrade, Serbia, is named after which pioneer of alternating-current electricity?
fact: Tesla's ashes are kept in a golden sphere at the Nikola Tesla Museum in Belgrade.

q: What is unusual about the location of Bratislava, the capital of Slovakia?
wrong: It lies on three large rivers
It sits in two time zones
fact: The city limits touch both Austria and Hungary, and Vienna is only about 60 km away.

q: Which mountains in Slovakia are often described as the smallest high-mountain range in the world?
fact: The main ridge is only about 26 km long, yet its highest peak, Gerlach, reaches 2,655 meters.

q: What does the coat of arms on the flag of Slovakia show?
answer: A double cross on three hills
wrong: A red eagle wearing a crown
fact: The hills are said to stand for the Tatra, Fatra and Mátra ranges - the last of which now lies in Hungary.

q: Which leader of American pop art had parents who emigrated from a village in what is now Slovakia?
fact: A museum devoted to him stands in the small town of Medzilaborce, near his parents' village of Miková.

q: Which pale, blind cave salamander, nicknamed the 'human fish', lives in the caves of Slovenia?
fact: Olms can live for around 100 years and survive for several years without food.

q: What stands on the small island in the middle of Lake Bled in Slovenia?
fact: Visitors climb 99 stone steps to reach it and ring its 'wishing bell'.

q: What are the blue and yellow of the flag of Ukraine commonly said to represent?
fact: Ukraine has long been called the breadbasket of Europe for its rich black soil.

q: Which beet soup is a national dish of Ukraine, added to a UNESCO heritage list in 2022?
fact: It is usually served with a spoonful of sour cream and garlic bread rolls called pampushky.

q: Who painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in Vatican City?
fact: He spent four years on it, from 1508 to 1512, working from scaffolding he designed himself.

q: Vatican City has the world's shortest national network of which kind of transport?
fact: The line opened in 1934. Only about 300 meters of track lie inside the country, entered through a gate in the Vatican wall.

q: Which country has the longest coastline in Europe, thanks to its fjords and islands?
fact: Counting every fjord and island, Norway's coast runs to more than 100,000 km.

q: Which country is nicknamed the 'Land of Fire and Ice' for its volcanoes and glaciers?
fact: It sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and has about 30 active volcanic systems, some of them under glaciers.

q: Which country lies entirely within the city of Rome?
fact: Its border is only about 3 km long, so you can walk around the whole country in under an hour.

q: Which of these countries produces the most olive oil?
fact: In most years Spain presses more olive oil than Italy and Greece combined, much of it in the province of Jaén.

q: In which country was Europe's oldest university founded, in 1088?
fact: The University of Bologna has been teaching without interruption ever since.

q: Greenland and the Faroe Islands are self-governing parts of which kingdom?
fact: Greenland alone is about 50 times larger than Denmark itself.

q: The white Lipizzaner horses are named after a stud farm founded in 1580. In which country does it lie today?
fact: Lipica was founded by the Habsburgs, and the breed still performs at the Spanish Riding School in Vienna.

q: Which country is home to the legend of William Tell, who shot an apple off his son's head?
fact: The story is set around 1307 and became a symbol of the country's struggle for independence.

q: Which country is the smallest member of the European Union by area?
fact: At 316 square km, the whole country is smaller than many European cities.

q: Which of these countries has the northernmost capital city?
fact: Reykjavik lies at 64 degrees north, just below the Arctic Circle.

q: In which country does a parliament called the Storting sit?
fact: The name means 'great assembly'. Sweden has the Riksdag and Denmark the Folketing.

q: Which country became the first in Europe to give women the right to vote, in 1906?
fact: Its women could also stand for election, and 19 of them won seats in parliament the following year.

q: Which country was the last in Europe to give women the vote in national elections, in 1984?
fact: The change passed by a narrow margin in a referendum in which only men could vote.

q: Which of these countries has the most UNESCO World Heritage Sites?
fact: Italy has more than 60 listed sites, from the historic center of Rome to the Dolomites.

q: Which of these countries drinks the most coffee per person?
fact: Finns get through roughly 10 kg of coffee per person each year - three to four cups a day.

q: Which country gave the world goulash, a stew spiced with paprika?
fact: It began as a meal cooked in kettles by cattle herders on the plains - 'gulyás' means herdsman.

q: In which country did Antonio Stradivari build his famous violins around 1700?
fact: He worked in the town of Cremona, and about 650 of his instruments still exist.

q: The croissant is modeled on the kipferl, a crescent-shaped pastry from which country?
fact: An Austrian baker opened a Viennese bakery in Paris around 1839, and the French made the pastry their own.

q: Which country is nicknamed the 'Emerald Isle' for its green countryside?
fact: Mild, wet Atlantic weather keeps its fields green all year round.

q: Which country's flag features an armillary sphere, a navigation tool from the Age of Discovery?
fact: The golden sphere sits behind the national shield and recalls the voyages of Portuguese explorers.

q: Which country's blue, white and red tricolor dates from its revolution of 1789?
fact: Blue and red were the colors of Paris, and white was the color of the king.

q: Roald Amundsen, leader of the first expedition to reach the South Pole, came from which country?
fact: His team arrived on December 14, 1911, about five weeks ahead of Britain's Robert Scott.

q: In which country does Aneto, the highest peak of the Pyrenees, stand?
fact: Aneto rises to 3,404 meters. Its glacier, long the largest in the Pyrenees, is melting fast and could be gone within decades.

q: In which country was the composer Frédéric Chopin born?
fact: He was born in the village of Żelazowa Wola in 1810 and left for Paris at 20. His heart rests in a Warsaw church.

q: Which country does tennis champion Novak Djokovic represent?
fact: He grew up in Belgrade and has won more Grand Slam singles titles than any other man.

q: Which country is home to the region of Transylvania?
fact: The name means 'the land beyond the forest', and the region is ringed by the Carpathian Mountains.

q: In which country is the European Central Bank based?
fact: It sits in Frankfurt and sets interest rates for the countries that use the euro.

q: In which country does the International Court of Justice, the main court of the United Nations, sit?
fact: The court works in the Peace Palace in The Hague, which opened in 1913.

q: Which microstate is perched on the slopes of Mount Titano?
fact: Three medieval towers crown the mountain's ridge, and all three appear on the country's flag.

q: Which country has the highest capital city in Europe, at about 1,000 meters above sea level?
fact: Andorra la Vella lies at 1,023 meters in a valley of the Pyrenees.

q: Which of these countries has the most islands - more than 200,000 of them?
fact: Sweden counts about 267,000 islands, though fewer than 1,000 of them are inhabited.

q: Which country is called Suomi in its own language?
fact: Nobody is sure where the name comes from. One theory links it to an old word for 'land'.

q: In which country's capital are the Nobel Prizes for physics, chemistry, medicine and literature presented?
fact: Only the Peace Prize is handed out elsewhere - in Oslo, as Alfred Nobel's will requested.

q: Which country supplies the colorfully dressed guards who have protected the pope since 1506?
fact: Recruits must be Swiss, Catholic and unmarried, and must have completed Swiss military training.

q: The Schengen Agreement on open borders is named after a village in which country?
fact: The 1985 agreement was signed on a riverboat on the Moselle, where Luxembourg meets France and Germany.

q: Which river flows through more countries than any other river in the world?
fact: The Danube passes through 10 countries on its way from Germany's Black Forest to the Black Sea.

q: What is the highest mountain in the Alps?
fact: It stands about 4,800 meters high on the border of France and Italy, and its exact height shifts with the ice on top.

q: Which is the longest river in Europe?
fact: It flows about 3,500 km through Russia to the Caspian Sea, never reaching an ocean.

q: Which mountain in the Caucasus is usually counted as the highest in Europe?
fact: Elbrus is a dormant volcano with two summits, the higher one reaching 5,642 meters.

q: How many gold stars are on the flag of the European Union?
fact: The number has nothing to do with the number of members - twelve was chosen as a symbol of completeness.

q: How many countries founded, in the 1950s, the community that later grew into the European Union?
fact: Belgium, France, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and West Germany signed the Treaty of Rome in 1957.

q: Which treaty, signed in 1992, formally created the European Union?
fact: Named after the Dutch city where it was signed, it also paved the way for the euro.

q: Which televised contest, first held in 1956, has European countries compete each year with an original song?
fact: Only seven countries took part in the first edition, held in Lugano, Switzerland.

q: Which black-and-white seabird with a colorful beak nests on North Atlantic cliffs from Iceland to Norway?
fact: Iceland has the largest colonies of all - millions of puffins nest there in clifftop burrows each summer.

q: The Sami are the indigenous people of which far-northern region of Europe?
fact: Their homeland, which they call Sápmi, stretches across Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia.

q: Which race completes cycling's three Grand Tours, alongside the Tour de France and the Giro d'Italia?
fact: First held in 1935, it is the youngest of the three, and its leader wears a red jersey.

q: Which Alpine dish is made by dipping bread into a shared pot of melted cheese?
fact: Its name comes from the French word 'fondre', meaning to melt.

q: Which competition, first played in 1955, is the top tournament for Europe's football clubs?
fact: It was called the European Cup until 1992, and Real Madrid won the first five editions.

q: How many European Union countries began using euro banknotes and coins on January 1, 2002?
fact: Germany's mark, France's franc and Italy's lira were among the currencies that disappeared within weeks.
